Last updated: November 21, 2026  |  Effective: November 21, 2026  |  Version 1.0
1. Emergency information
**If you think you are having a medical emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room right away.** Do not wait for a reply by email, chat, text message or the patient portal.
Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, chest pain or pressure, fainting, a seizure, or severe confusion.

**If you may have taken too much medication or used the wrong dose, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.** If the person collapses, has a seizure, has trouble breathing or cannot be woken up, call 911.
2. About this information

This page gives general safety information for adults who are prescribed one of the six products below through WellPeps, a Wyoming corporation (“WellPeps”). It does not replace your prescription label, your pharmacy’s instructions or your clinician’s advice.

**WellPeps is not a medical practice or a pharmacy.** WellPeps helps you reach telehealth services provided by independent licensed clinicians of OSI Medical Services, P.A. (the “Practice”). WellPeps does not prescribe, compound or dispense medication.

**A licensed clinician decides** whether a prescription is medically appropriate for you. A prescription is not guaranteed. A clinician may decline to prescribe, or may change or stop a prescription, at any time.
**A state-licensed pharmacy** named on your prescription label prepares and ships your medication.

**Your label comes first.** Ingredients, strengths, forms, syringes, storage rules and beyond-use dates can differ between prescriptions and between pharmacies. If this page and your label disagree, follow your label and contact your clinician or pharmacy.

3. Important: about compounded medicines
Every product in this document is a compounded medicine. A compounded medicine is made by a pharmacy for you, based on your prescriber’s order.

Compounded medicines are **not FDA-approved**. FDA does not review compounded medicines for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold. They do not come with FDA-approved labeling or an FDA Medication Guide. Strength, purity and quality can differ between pharmacies and between batches.
A compounded medicine is not a generic version of an FDA-approved medicine. Do not assume it is the same as, equivalent to or interchangeable with one.

**None of these six peptides is FDA-approved for any use, and none is an active ingredient in an FDA-approved medicine in the United States.** Do not assume a product is safe because it is sold by prescription or made by a licensed pharmacy.
Some of these peptides are versions or fragments of substances the body makes. That does not tell you what an injection, capsule or spray will do, or whether it is appropriate for you.

Because these products have not been through FDA review, their full risks, side effects, interactions and effectiveness may not be known. Some information below comes from general medical knowledge and from FDA-approved labeling for related products. That does not mean a compounded product behaves the same way.

The Compounded Medication Disclosure and Consent explains compounded medicines in more detail. You can ask your clinician at any time about other options, including no medicine at all. WellPeps does not offer brand-name FDA-approved products. FDA-approved medicines may be available through another provider and pharmacy.
4. What WellPeps does and does not claim

WellPeps does **not** claim that any product in this document treats, cures or prevents any disease or condition, speeds healing or recovery from an injury, builds muscle, improves memory or focus, changes your weight or metabolism, or slows aging. We do not promise any result. You may notice no change at all.
**What is known.** Each product contains substances that play a role in the body. A description of what a substance does in the body is not a promise of what an injection or capsule will do for you.

**What is not established.** For these peptides it has not been established that they are safe or that they give any benefit to people, for any use. Almost all of the research comes from lab studies and animal studies. Human studies are few, small and short, and for several of these peptides there are no published human safety studies at all. Long-term safety is unknown. FDA scientists who reviewed these peptides for compounding raised safety concerns, including the lack of human safety data (see each article).
If you see a statement from WellPeps that does not match this section, tell us at support@wellpeps.com.
5. Before you start, tell your clinician if you
have had an allergic reaction to any medicine, vitamin, preservative (such as benzyl alcohol), dye, latex or other ingredient.
are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding.
have or have had cancer or a tumor, or are being checked for one.
have diabetes or prediabetes, or take insulin or another diabetes medicine.
have heart disease, an irregular heartbeat, chest pain, or high or low blood pressure.
have kidney disease or liver disease.
have seizures, a blood disorder, a bleeding problem, or take a blood thinner.
have an autoimmune or inflammatory condition, or take medicine that affects your immune system.
have frequent nosebleeds, a nasal condition, or recent nose surgery (if you are prescribed Semax).
take any prescription or over-the-counter medicine, vitamin, supplement or herbal product. This includes medicines for depression, anxiety, ADHD, pain, migraine, sleep, cough and cold.
use any other peptide, hormone, injection, IV drip or “wellness” treatment from anywhere else.
are a competitive athlete or are subject to drug testing for sport, work or school. Several of these peptides are prohibited in sport.
6. Who should not use these products
Anyone who is not an adult. These products are for adults only. The minimum age depends on your state; see the Patient Terms of Service and Payment Agreement.
Anyone who is allergic to an ingredient on the label.
Anyone whose clinician decides the product is not appropriate. That is a medical decision, even if you want the product.
Anyone who falls under the “do not use” statements in the product article that applies to them.

8. Injection safety (Articles A, B, D and F)

This section applies to the injectable products. Your label and your pharmacy’s written instructions come first. If you have never injected yourself, ask for training through the patient portal before your first dose.
Use only the product, dose, route (under the skin or into a muscle), schedule and syringe on your current label.

**Units, milliliters (mL) and milligrams (mg) are not the same thing.** Syringes may be marked in units or mL, while a dose may be written in mg, mcg, mL or units. Mixing them up can cause a serious overdose. Before every injection, check the product name, the strength (amount per mL), your dose, the volume you will draw up and the markings on your syringe.
If any direction is missing, unclear or does not match another direction, do not inject until your clinician or the pharmacy confirms it.
A refill, or a different pharmacy, may have a different strength. Check your label every time. Never copy the number of “units” you used from a different vial.
Peptides often arrive as a powder that you mix before use. Mix only as your pharmacy instructs, with the diluent it supplied, and use the mixed product within the time on the label.
Do not mix products in one syringe or vial unless your clinician or pharmacy tells you to.

Wash your hands. Wipe the vial stopper and your skin with a new alcohol swab and let them dry. Use a new, sterile needle and syringe for every injection. Never touch the needle, and never reuse or share needles, syringes or vials.
Rotate injection sites. Do not inject into skin that is bruised, red, tender, scarred or hard.
Look at the liquid before every use. Do not use it if it is cloudy, discolored, frozen or has particles, unless your label says that is expected.
Do not leave a needle in a multi-dose vial. Throw the vial away after its beyond-use date even if liquid remains.
**These products are not for IV use at home.** Do not inject any of them into a vein. If your label says IV or “for office use,” do not use it yourself and contact your clinician.
9. Sharps disposal

Put used needles and syringes in an FDA-cleared sharps disposal container right after use. If you do not have one, use a heavy-duty, puncture-resistant household container with a tight lid, such as a laundry detergent bottle.
Do not throw loose needles or syringes in the trash or recycling, and do not flush them. Do not bend or break needles by hand.
Some states and towns do not allow sharps in household trash. Check your state and local rules. FDA’s sharps disposal information is at www.fda.gov/safesharpsdisposal.
Keep sharps and all medication out of reach of children and pets.
10. Storage, shipping and product quality

Follow your pharmacy label for refrigeration, room-temperature limits, protection from light and handling. Many injectable products must be kept cold. Do not freeze a product unless the label says to. Keep capsules and nasal sprays in their original containers, as the label says.

**Beyond-use date.** The pharmacy sets a date after which the product must not be used. Do not use it after that date, or after the time limit on the label for use after opening or mixing, even if some is left.

Some products must stay cold in transit. Open your package when it arrives and check it. If it arrives late, warm, with melted ice packs or was left in heat, contact the dispensing pharmacy before you use it. See the Shipping and Delivery Policy.
Do not use the product if the label is missing or incomplete, the seal is broken, the container is leaking or damaged, or the name or strength is not what you expected.
Do not assume storage guidance from an earlier shipment, another pharmacy or another product applies to your current prescription.
11. Pregnancy and breastfeeding

These products have not been well studied in pregnancy or breastfeeding, and some can harm an unborn baby. Tell your clinician before you start if you are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding, and tell your clinician right away if this changes. If you become pregnant while using one of these products, stop it and contact your clinician.
12. Other medicines, supplements and treatments

Tell your clinician about everything you take or use, including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, herbal products, and treatments from other places such as IV drips, injections at a spa or clinic, other peptides and hormones.

Do not “stack.” Do not use two of these products together, or with another peptide or similar product from anywhere else, unless your clinician has clearly told you to. Combinations of these peptides have not been studied for safety.

Do not buy or use peptides or other products labeled “for research use only” or “not for human consumption.” They are not made for people and may be contaminated, mislabeled or the wrong strength. WellPeps does not supply them. Peptides sold online for “research” are a common source of contaminated and mislabeled products.
If another clinician prescribes you a new medicine, tell them you use these products and tell your WellPeps clinician in the patient portal.
Some of these products may be banned under anti-doping or workplace drug-testing rules. If you are tested, you are responsible for checking the rules that apply to you.
13. Lab tests, follow-up and stopping
Your clinician tells you if labs are needed. Labs are billed separately. See the Laboratory Testing Consent.
You can stop at any time. Tell your clinician if you stop. Stopping does not by itself cancel your plan; see the Refund, Cancellation and Auto-Renewal Policy.
Do not change your dose, take it more often than prescribed or double a missed dose. If you miss a dose, follow your label or ask your clinician.
Your clinician may change or stop a prescription based on your health, test results, new medicines or changes in the rules for a product.
14. Questions and reporting problems
Non-emergency medical questions: message your prescribing clinician in the patient portal at portal.wellpeps.com.
Orders, shipping or billing help: support@wellpeps.com. Phone: (307) 881-8700, during normal business hours.
Ingredients, strength, preparation, storage or beyond-use date: the dispensing pharmacy listed on your prescription label.
To report a side effect or product-quality problem to FDA: FDA MedWatch at www.fda.gov/medwatch or 1-800-FDA-1088. Please also tell your clinician and the pharmacy.
15. Additional information

This is general information, not medical advice for you. It is not a complete list of warnings, risks, side effects, interactions or instructions. Your prescription label and the information from your dispensing pharmacy control if they differ from this summary. For general information about compounded drugs, see the “Human Drug Compounding” pages at www.fda.gov.
Product articles
Article A. BPC-157 injection
What it is
BPC-157 is a synthetic peptide made of 15 amino acids. Its sequence comes from a protein found in stomach juice. It is given as an injection under the skin.
FDA status

BPC-157 is not FDA-approved for any use. FDA has reviewed BPC-157 as an ingredient that pharmacies might compound, and FDA scientists raised safety concerns, including that the human studies are too small and too short to show it is safe or that it works for any use. The federal rules on whether and how pharmacies may compound BPC-157 have changed during 2026 and may change again. If they change, your clinician may stop or change your prescription.
What is known and what is not

Lab and animal studies have looked at BPC-157 and tissue repair, the stomach and gut, and blood-vessel growth. Very few small studies have been done in people. It is not known whether it helps people with any condition, what dose is safe, or what it does when used for months.
Do not use, or tell your clinician first, if you

have or have had cancer, a tumor or a growth that is being watched. These peptides are studied for effects on cell growth and blood-vessel growth, so they may not be appropriate if you have or have had cancer.
are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding. Do not use it then.
have a bleeding problem or take a blood thinner.
have heart disease or high or low blood pressure.
are a competitive athlete. BPC-157 is prohibited in sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).
Possible side effects
Redness, itching, swelling, bruising or a small lump where you inject.
Headache, dizziness, nausea, tiredness or flushing.
Side effects not listed here may happen, because it has not been well studied in people.
Stop and get help
Signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, hives over the body, or fainting. Call 911.
Chest pain, a fast or pounding heartbeat, fainting or severe dizziness. Call 911.
Signs of infection where you inject: spreading redness, warmth, pus, red streaks or fever. Contact your clinician right away.
A new lump or growth anywhere on your body, or any new symptom that worries you. Contact your clinician.
Medicines and products to tell your clinician about
Blood thinners and medicines that affect bleeding, including aspirin and ibuprofen.
Any other peptide, hormone or injection from anywhere else.
Article B. TB-500 injection
What it is
TB-500 is a synthetic peptide. It is a short fragment related to thymosin beta-4, a protein the body makes. It is given as an injection under the skin.
FDA status

TB-500 is not FDA-approved for any use. FDA has reviewed TB-500 as an ingredient that pharmacies might compound, and FDA scientists raised safety concerns, including that there are no published human safety studies. The federal rules on whether and how pharmacies may compound TB-500 have changed during 2026 and may change again. If they change, your clinician may stop or change your prescription.
What is known and what is not

Lab and animal studies have looked at thymosin beta-4 and its fragments in wound healing, tissue repair and blood-vessel growth. There are no published studies of TB-500 safety in people. It is not known whether it helps people with any condition, what dose is safe, or what it does over time.
Do not use, or tell your clinician first, if you

have or have had cancer, a tumor or a growth that is being watched. These peptides are studied for effects on cell growth and blood-vessel growth, so they may not be appropriate if you have or have had cancer.
are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding. Do not use it then.
have heart disease or a heart rhythm problem.
are a competitive athlete. TB-500 is prohibited in sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).
Possible side effects
Redness, itching, swelling, bruising or a small lump where you inject.
Headache, tiredness, light-headedness or flushing.
Side effects not listed here may happen, because it has not been studied in people.
Stop and get help
Signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, hives over the body, or fainting. Call 911.
Chest pain, a fast or pounding heartbeat, fainting or severe dizziness. Call 911.
Signs of infection where you inject: spreading redness, warmth, pus, red streaks or fever. Contact your clinician right away.
A new lump or growth anywhere on your body. Contact your clinician.
Medicines and products to tell your clinician about
Any other peptide, hormone or injection from anywhere else.
Article C. KPV capsules
What it is
KPV is a synthetic peptide of three amino acids. It is a fragment of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), a hormone the body makes. It is taken as capsules by mouth.
FDA status

KPV is not FDA-approved for any use. FDA has reviewed KPV as an ingredient that pharmacies might compound, and FDA scientists raised safety concerns, including that there are no published human safety studies. The federal rules on whether and how pharmacies may compound KPV have changed during 2026 and may change again. If they change, your clinician may stop or change your prescription.
What is known and what is not

Lab and animal studies have looked at KPV and inflammation in the gut and the skin. There are no published studies of KPV safety in people. It is not known whether it helps people with any condition or what it does over time.
Do not use, or tell your clinician first, if you
are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding. Do not use it then.

have an inflammatory bowel condition (such as Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis) or a skin condition. KPV is not a treatment for either, and it does not replace the treatment your doctor prescribed.
Possible side effects
Stomach upset, nausea, bloating or a change in bowel habits.
Headache or tiredness.
Side effects not listed here may happen, because it has not been studied in people.
Stop and get help
Signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, hives over the body, or fainting. Call 911.
Severe stomach pain, blood in your stool, or vomiting that does not stop. Get medical care right away.
A rash, itching or swelling after you start it. Stop taking it and contact your clinician.
Using it correctly
Take the capsules only by mouth, as your label says. Do not open or crush them unless your label says you may.
Medicines and products to tell your clinician about
Any medicine for an inflammatory bowel or skin condition.
Any other peptide or supplement you take.
Article D. MOTS-c injection
What it is
MOTS-c is a synthetic version of a small peptide made by mitochondria, the parts of a cell that produce energy. It is given as an injection under the skin.
FDA status

MOTS-c is not FDA-approved for any use. FDA has reviewed MOTS-c as an ingredient that pharmacies might compound, and FDA scientists raised safety concerns, including that there are no published human safety studies. The federal rules on whether and how pharmacies may compound MOTS-c have changed during 2026 and may change again. If they change, your clinician may stop or change your prescription.
What is known and what is not

Lab and animal studies have looked at MOTS-c and how the body uses energy and sugar. There are no published studies of MOTS-c safety in people. It is not known whether it helps people with any condition, what dose is safe, or what it does over time.
Do not use, or tell your clinician first, if you
are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding. Do not use it then.
have diabetes or prediabetes, or take insulin or another medicine that lowers blood sugar. MOTS-c may affect blood sugar.
have heart disease, kidney disease or liver disease.
Possible side effects
Redness, itching, swelling, bruising or a small lump where you inject.
Tiredness, headache, nausea or a fast heartbeat.
Low blood sugar if you take diabetes medicine: shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion or a fast heartbeat.
Side effects not listed here may happen, because it has not been studied in people.
Stop and get help
Signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, hives over the body, or fainting. Call 911.
Signs of very low blood sugar: confusion, fainting or a seizure. Call 911.
Chest pain, a fast or pounding heartbeat or fainting. Call 911.
Medicines and products to tell your clinician about
Insulin and every medicine you take for diabetes or blood sugar, including GLP-1 medicines.
Any other peptide, hormone or injection from anywhere else.
Article E. Semax nasal spray
What it is
Semax is a synthetic peptide of seven amino acids, based on part of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), a hormone the body makes. It is used as a nasal spray.
FDA status

Semax is not FDA-approved for any use. FDA has reviewed Semax as an ingredient that pharmacies might compound, and FDA scientists raised safety concerns, including that the evidence about its safety is limited. The federal rules on whether and how pharmacies may compound Semax have changed during 2026 and may change again. If they change, your clinician may stop or change your prescription.
What is known and what is not

Semax has been studied mainly in Russia, where it is registered as a medicine, and in lab and animal studies. Most human studies are small. It is not approved in the United States. It is not known whether it helps healthy people with memory, focus or anything else, or what it does over time.
Do not use, or tell your clinician first, if you
are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding. Do not use it then.
have seizures or epilepsy.
have bipolar disorder, anxiety, or trouble sleeping.
have high blood pressure or heart disease.
have frequent nosebleeds, a nasal condition or recent nose surgery.
Possible side effects
Irritation, dryness or a runny nose, or nosebleeds.
Headache, trouble sleeping, feeling restless, jittery or anxious.
Side effects not listed here may happen, because it has not been well studied.
Stop and get help
Signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, hives over the body, or fainting. Call 911.
A seizure. Call 911.
Severe headache, chest pain or a fast or pounding heartbeat. Get medical care right away.
Changes in mood or behavior that worry you or the people around you. Contact your clinician.
Using it correctly
Use it only in the nose, in the number of sprays and on the schedule your label says.
Do not share the bottle. Wipe the tip after use and replace the cap.
If your nose bleeds or becomes very sore, stop using it and contact your clinician.
Medicines and products to tell your clinician about
Medicines for depression, anxiety, ADHD, seizures or sleep, and stimulants (including caffeine pills).
Nasal sprays you use for allergies or congestion.
Article F. Epitalon injection
What it is
Epitalon (also written epithalon) is a synthetic peptide of four amino acids, based on a substance from the pineal gland, a small gland in the brain. It is given as an injection under the skin.
FDA status

Epitalon is not FDA-approved for any use. FDA has reviewed Epitalon as an ingredient that pharmacies might compound, and FDA scientists raised safety concerns, including that there are no published human safety studies. The federal rules on whether and how pharmacies may compound Epitalon have changed during 2026 and may change again. If they change, your clinician may stop or change your prescription.
What is known and what is not

Epitalon has been studied mainly in lab and animal studies, mostly in Russia, for effects on cell aging and sleep cycles. There are no published human safety studies of the kind FDA relies on. It is not known whether it helps people with sleep, aging or any condition, or what it does over time.
Do not use, or tell your clinician first, if you

have or have had cancer, a tumor or a growth that is being watched. These peptides are studied for effects on cell growth and blood-vessel growth, so they may not be appropriate if you have or have had cancer.
are pregnant, may be pregnant, plan to become pregnant or are breastfeeding. Do not use it then.
take medicine for sleep, or have a sleep disorder.
Possible side effects
Redness, itching, swelling, bruising or a small lump where you inject.
Changes in sleep, drowsiness, headache or tiredness.
Side effects not listed here may happen, because it has not been studied in people.
Stop and get help
Signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, hives over the body, or fainting. Call 911.
Signs of infection where you inject: spreading redness, warmth, pus, red streaks or fever. Contact your clinician right away.
A new lump or growth anywhere on your body. Contact your clinician.
Medicines and products to tell your clinician about
Sleep medicines, melatonin and other products for sleep.
Any other peptide, hormone or injection from anywhere else.
